title: N-Ch-M

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-A-L: the go'el, who walks to the gate and buys back what was lost. Your line was redeem. Today, what family does when the loss can't be bought back.

A house with the mirrors covered. The front door is left unlocked so nobody has to ring. Inside, the mourners sit on low stools, and visitors come in quietly with trays of food and sit near them. By an old custom, the visitors don't start talking. They wait, sometimes a long while, until the mourner speaks first. Leaving, they say a set line in Hebrew, something like: may God, called here the Place, comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. The verb in that line, yenachem, comes from today's root.
screen: `A SHIVA HOUSE.` → `THE VISITORS WAIT.` → `MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.`

segments.voice: N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem. Nechamah, comfort. Turn it four ways. First, the prophet. Isaiah chapter forty opens: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." In Hebrew, nachamu, nachamu: said twice, as if once weren't enough. That chapter is read on the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, and that Shabbat takes its name from the first word: Shabbat Nachamu. Second, a baby's name. When Noah is born, his father Lamech explains the name: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands." The text ties the boy's name to comfort, after the curse on the ground that made work so hard. Third, Joseph. After Jacob dies, his brothers are afraid Joseph will finally pay them back for selling him. Instead, "he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them." More literally, he spoke to their heart: not a speech about what went wrong, but words aimed at the heart. Fourth, the shiva house, which you sat in earlier this year. Yenachem, may God comfort you. The visitors don't claim to do the comforting themselves. They sit, they wait, they bring food, and they hand the comfort back to the Place. A prophet's doubled cry, a baby's name, a brother's kind words, a quiet visit: one root.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy, a loss, an illness, a job gone, a quiet loneliness, and picture yourself sitting near them the way visitors sit at a shiva: not fixing, not explaining, just there. Think of a few words aimed at the heart, the way Joseph spoke to his brothers, and hold them until they feel right; if you pray, you can ask that they be comforted. And if the heavy thing is yours, and you're in danger or thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem: nechamah, comfort, from nachamu to yenachem. This week's roots ran soul, earth, keep, work, king, redeem, and comfort. Today's word.
Your line: comfort. Sometimes it's simply being there, with words aimed at the heart. Go gently.

notes: Quotations from the KJV; JPS 1917 Isaiah 40:1 reads 'Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God.' Confirm the Judaism path accepts KJV.
Moed Katan 28b: comforters may not speak until the mourner opens; paraphrased as 'an old custom' and 'the Talmud teaches'. Confirm.

The shiva phrase (ha-Makom yenachem etchem b'toch she'ar avelei Tziyon v'Yerushalayim) paraphrased; 'many say' describes a common custom, not a statistic. Covered mirrors and unlocked doors are customs, not universal; soften if needed.
Genesis 50:21 'spake kindly unto them' is vaydaber al libam, literally 'spoke to/upon their heart'; confirm.
Genesis 5:29 ties Noah's name to comfort (yenachamenu); the script says only that the text ties them.
Tisha b'Av described as 'the day of mourning for the Temples'; Shabbat Nachamu's haftarah is Isaiah 40:1–26.
